newsitem.title: CUBA: Canada, Cuba agree to move dialogue forward.
newsitem.headline: Canada, Cuba agree to move dialogue forward.

text.p: Canada and Cuba agreed during a brief visit by Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy on Wednesday to move their dialogue forward on a range of issues that will include human rights.

Axworthy, who held talks with Cuban President Fidel Castro on Tuesday evening and over lunch on Wednesday during his 24-hour visit, said the two countries now had some concrete steps to work on in the coming months.
A joint declaration approved by Axworthy and his Cuban counterpart Roberto Robaina noted 14 points spanning political and economic themes where the two countries will aim for closer cooperation.

These include "broadening and deepening cooperation on the issue of human rights," including seminars and academic exchanges; cooperation in the area of justice, such as exchanges of judges and judicial training; exchanges relating to Cuba's intention to strengthen a Citizens' Complaints Commission; and increased support for Cuban and Canadian non-governmental organisations.

While these steps may not herald major changes in Cuba, it was significant that Havana, which normally bridles at criticism of its one-party system, agreed publicly to address such issues and to cooperate on them with a foreign country.

Axworthy, speaking at a joint news conference with Robaina just before leaving for Ottowa, implictly put this down to what he called the "Canadian way of doing things, neither European nor U.S." He added that Canada believed change could be encouraged through "active engagement and dialogue."
"It's a good beginning. These are concrete points to be followed up in the coming months," Axworthy said.
Axworthy's visit has highlighted Canada's difference over Cuba policy with the United States, which has long favoured isolating Castro's government.
Robaina said there were no taboo subjects for Cuba as long as it was treated with respect.
In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, asked about the declaration, said "We'll look at it very closely, and if appropriate, have something to say perhaps tomorrow."

He said the United States remained "skeptical that the Cuban government is in fact prepared to take systematic and meaningful steps that would lead toward ... a transition to democratic rule in Cuba. Or (steps) that would reflect a change in the position of the Cuban government on human rights."
Robaina made clear that however respectfully criticisms were made, Cuba will accept lessons from nobody. "Human rights in Cuba are the responsibility of Cubans," he said.
Apart from talking to Castro, Axworthy on Wednesday accompanied deputy president Carlos Lage on a visit to oil wells and hotels at Varadero, 90 miles (148 km) east of Havana.

Canadian firms, particularly in mining and tourism, have been among the leaders in foreign companies investing in Cuba after the island began a drive to attract foreign capital five years ago. Canada is also a leading trade partner of Cuba and Canadians are among the largest group of foreign tourists to the island.

Washington has long sought to isolate Cuba and last year toughened its 35-year-old economic embargo with its Helms-Burton law, which includes penalties on some third country firms doing business with Cuba. Ottawa has been a leading opponent of the law.
However, Axworthy said his visit to Cuba was not in order to make any point about the law.
